I’m learning French and I want to practise a natural conversation focused on **Quand quelqu’un donne un avis hyper définitif sur quelque chose qu’il connaît à peine**, as part of expressing opinions, reactions, agreement and disagreement.

Please speak to me in **natural, everyday French**.

Create a realistic conversation that naturally gives me opportunities to express the kinds of ideas covered in this section of my course. For example:

- He has a very strong opinion for someone who doesn’t really know the subject.
- He read two tweets and now he’s an expert.
- Maybe get informed before being that categorical.
- I always find certainty without knowledge fascinating.
- The less he knows, the more certain he is.
- People who really know the subject tend to be much more nuanced.
- Everything is simple to him.
- I’m always wary of overly simple answers to complicated problems.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural.

Where appropriate, **have an opinion of your own**. Don’t automatically agree with me. Sometimes challenge me lightly, take a different view, question my reasoning, or give me a new angle so I have a genuine reason to agree, disagree, qualify my opinion or change my mind.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

PROMPT 237 — Quand quelqu’un lance des piques en prétendant plaisanter
============================================================================

I’m learning French and I want to practise a natural conversation focused on **Quand quelqu’un lance des piques en prétendant plaisanter**, as part of expressing opinions, reactions, agreement and disagreement.

Please speak to me in **natural, everyday French**.

Create a realistic conversation that naturally gives me opportunities to express the kinds of ideas covered in this section of my course. For example:

- Ah, the famous “joke.”
- A joke is normally funny for both people.
- Otherwise it’s just a dig.
- You can’t excuse everything with “I was joking.”
- Humour doesn’t give you a free pass.
- But you have to know the limit.
- And especially notice when the other person stops laughing.
- It’s just being annoying.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural.

Where appropriate, **have an opinion of your own**. Don’t automatically agree with me. Sometimes challenge me lightly, take a different view, question my reasoning, or give me a new angle so I have a genuine reason to agree, disagree, qualify my opinion or change my mind.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Create a realistic conversation that naturally gives me opportunities to express the kinds of ideas covered in this section of my course. For example:

- She cancels all the time.
- You can never really rely on the plan happening.
- Once, obviously.
- But when it’s constant…
- It becomes a habit.
- I find that fairly selfish.
- I’d much rather have a clear no.
- Eventually I stop suggesting plans.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural.

Where appropriate, **have an opinion of your own**. Don’t automatically agree with me. Sometimes challenge me lightly, take a different view, question my reasoning, or give me a new angle so I have a genuine reason to agree, disagree, qualify my opinion or change my mind.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

- “I don’t like gossip.”
- And yet you know everything about everyone.
- But she wants every detail.
- Purely out of scientific curiosity, obviously.
- Might as well own it.
- The problem isn’t necessarily enjoying gossip.
- Being curious is human.
- Being malicious is something else.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural.

Where appropriate, **have an opinion of your own**. Don’t automatically agree with me. Sometimes challenge me lightly, take a different view, question my reasoning, or give me a new angle so I have a genuine reason to agree, disagree, qualify my opinion or change my mind.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

- Maybe I’m old-fashioned, but I ask.
- I really struggle with that level of cheek.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural.

Where appropriate, **have an opinion of your own**. Don’t automatically agree with me. Sometimes challenge me lightly, take a different view, question my reasoning, or give me a new angle so I have a genuine reason to agree, disagree, qualify my opinion or change my mind.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Where appropriate, **have an opinion of your own**. Don’t automatically agree with me. Sometimes challenge me lightly, take a different view, question my reasoning, or give me a new angle so I have a genuine reason to agree, disagree, qualify my opinion or change my mind.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend with actual opinions, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Use everyday subjects people actually have opinions about: music, films and TV, food, clothes, prices, places, habits, social situations, parenting, purchases, trends, annoying behaviour, relationships, stories, recommendations and whatever else fits this particular context.

Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

==================================================================================

Keep everyday French life, getting dressed, clothes shopping, fit, style, shoes, appearance, laundry, hair, makeup and real-life clothing situations in mind where relevant.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural. Keep everyday French life, getting dressed, clothes shopping, fit, style, shoes, appearance, laundry, hair, makeup and real-life clothing situations in mind where relevant.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

- It needs a genuinely nice café.
- There’s a stop just downstairs/outside.
- We’re next to the main square.
- It’s on the other side of the square.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural. Keep everyday French life, neighbourhoods, cafés, restaurants, bars, parks, local shops, housing and places people actually go in mind where relevant.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, pronunciation-style wording issue, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural. Keep everyday French life, neighbourhoods, cafés, restaurants, bars, parks, local shops, housing and places people actually go in mind where relevant.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, pronunciation-style wording issue, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, pronunciation-style wording issue, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, pronunciation-style wording issue, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Please speak to me in **natural, everyday French**.

Create a realistic conversation that naturally gives me opportunities to express the kinds of ideas covered in this part of my course. For example:

- Does he go to nursery?
- He’s starting the first year of maternelle.
- It mattered to me to have the school nearby.
- Have you heard good things about it?
- It’s the local catchment school.
- Is there before-school care?
- What time does morning childcare start?
- Do you close during the school holidays?

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural. Keep everyday French life, neighbourhoods, cafés, restaurants, bars, parks, local shops, housing and places people actually go in mind where relevant.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, pronunciation-style wording issue, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Create a realistic conversation that naturally gives me opportunities to express the kinds of ideas covered in this part of my course. For example:

- Until what time do you have to pay?

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural. Keep everyday French life, neighbourhoods, cafés, restaurants, bars, parks, local shops, housing and places people actually go in mind where relevant.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, pronunciation-style wording issue, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Keep everyday French transport and travel in mind where relevant: walking, métro, RER, buses, SNCF trains, stations, directions, delays, tickets, meeting people, getting home, taxis/VTCs, cycling and real-life travel hassles.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

I’m learning French and I want to practise a natural conversation about **Finding an address / apartment building**, as part of getting around and everyday transport.

Please speak to me in **natural, everyday French**.

This section of my course is specifically about:
**Finding an address / apartment building: Trying to find an address: asking the person to send the direct Maps link.**

Create a realistic conversation that naturally gives me opportunities to express the kinds of ideas covered in this section. For example:

- Just send me the link.

You do not need to cover every example, and you can introduce closely related situations if they make the conversation feel more natural. Keep everyday French transport and travel in mind where relevant: walking, métro, RER, buses, SNCF trains, stations, directions, delays, tickets, meeting people, getting home, taxis/VTCs, cycling and real-life travel hassles.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.

Have a real back-and-forth conversation with me rather than giving me exercises. Ask me **one question at a time**, respond naturally to what I actually say, and let the conversation develop organically. Use realistic everyday situations and follow whatever details I give you rather than mechanically working through a checklist.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.

Use **natural, informal everyday French as people actually speak it**, especially the kind of French you would hear in ordinary conversation in and around Paris. Use normal spoken contractions, reactions, discourse markers and filler words. Don’t force slang into every sentence, but don’t sound like a textbook.

In normal informal speech, don’t systematically use formal written constructions such as full **ne...pas** or inverted questions unless the situation genuinely calls for them. Prefer the way people actually speak.

Don’t simplify your French unnaturally. If I don’t understand something, I’ll ask.

Do **not** tell me the French translations of the ideas above before I answer. They are there to guide the conversation, not to give me the answers. I want to retrieve the French myself.

**CORRECTION RULE — IMPORTANT**

After **every sentence I say**, check whether it needs correcting.

- If there is a grammatical mistake, incorrect word, gender/agreement problem, unnatural construction, or something a French person would normally phrase differently, **briefly correct it first**.
- Give me the corrected / more natural French.
- Keep the correction concise.
- Then immediately respond naturally to what I said and continue the conversation with an appropriate response or follow-up question.
- If my sentence is already natural and correct, **do not mention that it is correct**. Simply respond and continue.
- Do not praise every correct sentence.
- Do not save corrections until later.
- Do not give me a list of corrections at the end.
- Do not interrupt the flow with a long grammar explanation unless I specifically ask why.

If I stop mid-sentence because I don’t know a French word and ask how to say something, just tell me the natural French word or phrase and let me finish what I was saying.

If I use an English word inside a French sentence because I don’t know the French, give me the natural French equivalent and let me continue.

Don’t translate your French into English unless I ask.

Most importantly: **talk to me like a French friend having a real conversation, not like a teacher conducting a speaking exam.**

Start the conversation now in French.
